ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: ; June 03–05, 2018; Woodstock, NYISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06
Wenhao Li, Qinglin Jia, Chenghou Jin, Zihong Xian, Jiezhou Ji, Yanzhi Liu, Zezheng Wang,
Bo Chen, Ruiming Tang, Chaoyi Ma†, Zhaojie Liu†, Wenwu Ou† Affiliation: Kuaishou Technology, Beijing, China email: liwenhao05, machaoyi03, zhaotianxing, luocheng10@kuaishou.com
Received  5 June 2009
Abstract.

Modeling lifetime user behavior sequences is essential for capturing long-range preferences in industrial recommendation, yet 100K-length user sequences make target-aware ranking prohibitively expensive. Search-based methods that retrieve from raw sequences incur candidate-dependent costs that grow with sequence length, whereas latent compression methods reduce computation at the expense of item-level addressability. We propose ECHO (Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators), a framework that balances efficiency and fine-grained retrieval by retaining a subset of original event records per user via a Distilled Selector (DS) and retrieving a smaller set of target-relevant records per candidate via a Target-aware Fine-grained Retriever (TFR). DS is supervised by a candidate-aware full-history teacher via per-target distillation, enabling target-aware user-level selection without incurring full-history computation for every candidate. The retriever and target-attention scorer share the teacher’s learned relevance parameters, ensuring consistent relevance estimation across the cascade. At a sequence length of L=100​KL=100\mathrm{K}, ECHO reduces online sequence-branch FLOPs by approximately 160×160\times compared with a representative end-to-end model. Three deployment optimizations—common user inputs, compact record encoding, and key-side projection absorption—further reduce memory, storage, and data-movement overhead. Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and an industrial-scale short-video platform demonstrate relative GAUC improvements of 0.113%0.113\%–1.520%1.520\% over state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines across multiple tasks. Furthermore, online A/B testing in two production scenarios, Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite, shows that ECHO improves app usage time by +0.240%+0.240\% and +0.373%+0.373\%, respectively.

Keywords: 
Recommender Systems, User Behavior Modeling, Knowledge Distillation

1. Introduction

In industrial-scale short-video recommendation, user interactions continuously accumulate into long behavior sequences that provide rich and diverse evidence for modeling users’ evolving preferences (Deng et al., 2025; He et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2026). For active users on Kuaishou, these sequences can easily reach 10410^{4} events within a single month. Such histories capture not only recent intent but also stable preferences, recurring interests, and infrequent interests that may be difficult to identify from short behavioral windows (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2025). Effectively exploiting these long-term behavioral signals has therefore become an important direction for improving ranking performance in large-scale industrial recommendation (Chen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2024).

However, directly modeling raw behavior sequences during ranking is prohibitively expensive (Ding et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025). A ranking request typically needs to score multiple candidate items for the same user, and target-aware history modeling must evaluate historical behaviors with respect to each individual candidate (Huang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026a). As user behavior sequences grow to 10510^{5} events or more, this candidate-dependent computation becomes prohibitively expensive under strict industrial latency and throughput constraints.

To make long-history modeling practical, a line of search-based methods adopts a two-stage paradigm. A lightweight General Search Unit (GSU) first retrieves a small subset of target-relevant behaviors from the long history, and an Exact Search Unit (ESU) then applies more expressive target attention over the retrieved behaviors. Representative methods such as SIM and TWIN (Pi et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2023) are attractive because they preserve the original item records selected from the user’s history. The downstream ranker can therefore still perform fine-grained target-to-item matching and trace its evidence back to concrete historical behaviors. However, the GSU must still search over the original behavior sequence for each candidate, causing its online computation cost to grow with the sequence length. Consequently, scaling search-based methods to histories containing around 100K events remains challenging under real-world industrial ranking constraints.

Another line of work reduces the cost of ultra-long history modeling through compression. These methods summarize user histories into a compact set of latent states, sketches, or interest vectors, and perform target-conditioned reasoning over the compressed representations (Wang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026a). SequenceO1 (Guan et al., 2026a), for example, scales to sequences of up to 100K events using a fixed-size user-only sketch and cache reuse, alongside a recent-history branch. Its sketch branch bounds candidate-dependent computation without repeatedly scanning the full history. However, compressing diverse behaviors into a finite-capacity representation before observing the target may blend interest-specific details and attenuate sparse behavioral evidence. This is a particular concern for users with dispersed interests or long-tail targets whose relevance depends on only a few historical interactions. Within the compressed sketch, such interactions are no longer individually searchable. Retaining original records offers an alternative, allowing downstream matching to directly access the concrete behaviors that survive selection.

A natural way to combine the advantages of the two directions is to first compress the search space and then retrieve from it. TWIN V2 (Si et al., 2024) demonstrates this paradigm by compressing lifelong behaviors in a target-independent manner, retaining a single representative item for each cluster, and subsequently performing online retrieval with cluster-aware target attention. This design extends the searchable range beyond what a direct GSU can efficiently handle. However, because the first-stage compression is target-independent and retains only one item per cluster, the original behaviors grouped into the same cluster are no longer independently accessible to the online retriever. This motivates us to explore a complementary form of compression that reduces the search space while preserving the original event records.

Our goal is to shorten the history before target-aware ranking while preserving as much prediction-relevant evidence of user interests as possible and keeping retained behaviors individually searchable. We pursue this goal by selecting original event records with their item identities and side features intact, guided by relevance signals learned from downstream prediction rather than solely by recency heuristics or offline structure.

We propose ECHO, a distillation-guided framework for lifetime behavior modeling with item-level evidence. Its name stands for Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators. During training, a user-level Distilled Selector (DS) retains KK original event records from each user’s history and materializes them for reuse across requests and candidates. For each target item, a Target-aware Fine-grained Retriever (TFR) searches only the retained records and selects at most MM behaviors for final interest aggregation. With K=10,000K=10{,}000 and M=100M=100 in our production setting, candidate-dependent online computation is confined to the retained history rather than the full 100K-event sequence. The selector is supervised by a candidate-aware full-history teacher trained with the prediction objective. Following TWIN’s scoring-consistency strategy (Chang et al., 2023), the retriever and target-attention scorer also share the teacher’s learned relevance parameters, aligning selection supervision with downstream matching.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose ECHO, a distillation-guided cascade that combines user-level selection with target-aware retrieval to efficiently model lifetime user behaviors. By distilling target-aware relevance from a full-history teacher and retaining original event records with their item identities and side features intact, ECHO enables candidate-specific matching while preserving item-level addressability.

  • •

    We reduce online sequence-branch FLOPs by approximately 160×160\times relative to a representative end-to-end model at L=100​KL=100\mathrm{K}, and describe three deployment optimizations that reduce memory, storage, and data-movement costs.

  • •

    Extensive experiments on KuaiRand-1K and an industrial-scale short-video platform demonstrate relative GAUC improvements of 0.113%0.113\%–1.520%1.520\% over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple tasks. Online A/B testing in Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite further shows improvements of +0.240%+0.240\% and +0.373%+0.373\% in app usage time, respectively.

2. Related Work

Existing long-sequence models can be broadly categorized as end-to-end, retrieval-based, compression-based, and hybrid methods (Zhou et al., 2026b).

End-to-end long-sequence modeling. These methods directly extend the ranker’s capacity for longer histories. LONGER (Chai et al., 2025) reduces sequence length through cross-attention before deeper self-attention, STCA (Guan et al., 2026b) combines stacked target-to-history cross-attention with batching and length extrapolation, and HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024) improves efficiency through specialized attention operators and sample organization. However, because these methods directly process the input history, their computational cost grows approximately linearly with sequence length, making them difficult to scale to 100K-level histories.

Retrieval-based long-sequence modeling. These methods retrieve target-relevant records before fine-grained interest modeling. SIM (Pi et al., 2020) establishes this paradigm, ETA (Chen et al., 2021) accelerates retrieval through approximate matching, and TWIN (Chang et al., 2023) aligns the relevance metrics used in retrieval and downstream attention. TransAct V2 (Xia et al., 2025) strengthens interactions among retrieved behaviors, while MUSE (Wu et al., 2025) incorporates multimodal semantics. Although preserving item-level access, these methods search the long history for each candidate, leaving online cost dependent on sequence length.

Compression-based methods. These methods summarize ultra-long histories into compact representations to bound candidate-dependent computation. C-Former (Wang et al., 2025) and DV365 (Lyu et al., 2025) learn compact interest states or progressively reduced representations, while SequenceO1 (Guan et al., 2026a) supports histories of up to 100K events through a fixed-size user-only sketch, cache reuse, and recent-history modeling. Although efficient, such compression may limit item-level access and discard sparse target-relevant evidence when the representation is constructed before the target is observed.

Hybrid retrieval-and-compression methods. These methods combine search and compression to balance efficiency and effectiveness. DILN (Cai et al., 2025) first selects interactions by action type and then compresses the resulting subsequences with CNN-based encoders. In contrast, TWIN V2 (Si et al., 2024) compresses lifelong behaviors into cluster-structured representations before cluster-aware target retrieval. ADFM (Li et al., 2022) pre-selects and stores top-kk behaviors for reuse during inference. While reducing online computation, these methods may limit item-level access or omit target-relevant evidence when their offline selection or compression criteria differ from downstream relevance.

3. Methodology

3.1. Problem Formulation

Let vv denote a target item, and let ℋ=((xj,τj))j=1L\mathcal{H}=((x_{j},\tau_{j}))_{j=1}^{L} denote the user’s chronologically ordered lifetime behavior sequence, where LL is the sequence length, xjx_{j} contains the item identity and side features of the jj-th historical event, and τj\tau_{j} is its timestamp. Repeated interactions with the same item occupy distinct sequence positions. Given the user and request context cc, target features xvx_{v}, and history ℋ\mathcal{H}, the ranker estimates the probability of each behavior label y(t)y^{(t)} for task tt. We focus on ultra-long histories with lengths on the order of 10510^{5}, as considered in recent work (Guan et al., 2026a).

Throughout, CC denotes the number of target items scored per request, KK the number of original event records retained by the user-level selector, and MM the number of records passed to final interest aggregation, where M≪K≪LM\ll K\ll L.

3.2. Framework Overview

ECHO is an end-to-end framework that connects real-time sequence selection with target-aware ranking through two nested budgets (Figure 1). In Figure 1(a), during real-time training, a Distilled Selector (DS) scores each user’s lifetime history using user features independent of the candidate item and writes KK retained event records to an intermediate store. The ranking graph in Figure 1(b) reads these records during both training and online inference. A Target-aware Fine-grained Retriever (TFR) selects MM records for each target using TWIN-style retrieval (Chang et al., 2023), and Candidate-aware Interest Aggregation summarizes them for the multi-task ranker. Online requests only read the retained history; they do not execute DS or rescan the full sequence. A typical configuration in our system uses K=10,000K=10{,}000 and M=100M=100.

3.3. User-Level Sequence Compression

DS reduces the searchable history from LL to KK before target-aware ranking; the empirical basis for compressing 10510^{5}-level histories to 10410^{4} retained records is examined in Sec. 4.3. Its input aa contains only user features, such as user identity embeddings, and does not depend on the candidate item. The selection is user-only, so the stored records are reused across requests and candidates.

3.3.1. Selection

DS embeds each historical event from its features and timestamp as zjS=fhistS​(xj,τj)z^{S}_{j}=f^{S}_{\mathrm{hist}}(x_{j},\tau_{j}) and the user from profile features aa as e=fuser​(a)e=f_{\mathrm{user}}(a). The score is the mean inner product over HsH_{s} heads:

(1) sjS=1Hs​∑h=1Hs⟨WQ,hS​e,WK,hS​zjS⟩.s^{S}_{j}=\frac{1}{H_{s}}\sum_{h=1}^{H_{s}}\bigl\langle W^{S}_{Q,h}e,\;W^{S}_{K,h}z^{S}_{j}\bigr\rangle.

All equations range over real events; padded positions in batched tensors are masked out of selection and normalization. DS retains the highest-scoring positions,

(2) ℐK=Top​-​Kj∈[1,L]⁡(sjS),ℋ~=((xj,τj))j∈ℐK,\mathcal{I}^{K}=\operatorname*{Top\text{-}K}_{j\in[1,L]}(s^{S}_{j}),\qquad\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}=\bigl((x_{j},\tau_{j})\bigr)_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{K}},

where ℐK\mathcal{I}^{K} is a score-ordered list of event positions. Unlike latent-token compression, which represents history through mixtures of features, this operation retains original records with their item IDs, timestamps, and side features intact. They remain individually addressable for downstream target-to-item matching, including evidence for long-tail targets and dispersed interests.

3.3.2. Target-aware distillation

A selector conditioned only on user features cannot adapt to the target, yet relevance in ranking is target-dependent. We bridge this gap with a candidate-aware teacher trained over the full history in the selector graph. The teacher uses its own event encoder zjT=fhistT​(xj,τj)z^{T}_{j}=f^{T}_{\mathrm{hist}}(x_{j},\tau_{j}), with embeddings and transformations independent of the student’s. For each training target vv, it averages relevance logits over HtH_{t} heads:

(3) sv,jT=1Ht​∑h=1Ht⟨WQ,hT​fT​(c,xv),WK,hT​zjT⟩,s^{T}_{v,j}=\frac{1}{H_{t}}\sum_{h=1}^{H_{t}}\bigl\langle W^{T}_{Q,h}f_{T}(c,x_{v}),\;W^{T}_{K,h}z^{T}_{j}\bigr\rangle,

where fTf_{T} encodes context and target features. Distillation aligns the student’s selection with the teacher’s per-target relevance.

Distribution matching.

For a batch ℬ\mathcal{B}, let bb index a user–target sample with user ubu_{b}, target vbv_{b}, and history length LbL_{b}. Write sb,jTs^{T}_{b,j} for Eq. (3) evaluated at vbv_{b}, and sb,jSs^{S}_{b,j} for the user-only student score of ubu_{b}, which Eq. (1) shares across all samples of that user. With temperature TT, we define pb,jT=softmaxj⁡(sb,jT/T)p^{T}_{b,j}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j}(s^{T}_{b,j}/T) and pb,jS=softmaxj⁡(sb,jS/T)p^{S}_{b,j}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j}(s^{S}_{b,j}/T). These normalized distributions correspond to the teacher and student attention weights in Figure 1(a), rather than the raw relevance logits. The distillation loss is

(4) ℒKD=−T2|ℬ|∑b∈ℬ∑j=1Lbsg[pb,jT]logpb,jS,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}=-\frac{T^{2}}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{b}}\operatorname{sg}[p^{T}_{b,j}]\log p^{S}_{b,j},

where sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. Rather than using only a binary indication of whether each record belongs to the teacher’s Top-KK, the soft targets encode how strongly the teacher prefers each position in the history.

Boundary-targeted auxiliary term.

Matching the full distribution can still leave teacher-preferred records outside the student’s Top-KK. We therefore add a ranking objective across the selection boundary: it raises the student scores of missed records preferred by the teacher relative to those of less relevant retained records, encouraging their inclusion in the selected history.

For each sample bb, form a sharper teacher distribution p~bT=softmax⁡(sbT/Tm)\tilde{p}^{T}_{b}=\operatorname{softmax}(s^{T}_{b}/T_{m}), with Tm<TT_{m}<T. Against the user’s student-selected set ℐubK\mathcal{I}^{K}_{u_{b}}, mine up to nn positions in each region:

(5) (jb,1+,…)\displaystyle(j^{+}_{b,1},\ldots) =Top​-​nj∉ℐubK⁡(p~b,jT),\displaystyle=\operatorname*{Top\text{-}n}_{j\notin\mathcal{I}^{K}_{u_{b}}}(\tilde{p}^{T}_{b,j}),
(jb,1−,…)\displaystyle(j^{-}_{b,1},\ldots) =Top​-​nj∈ℐubK⁡(−p~b,jT).\displaystyle=\operatorname*{Top\text{-}n}_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{K}_{u_{b}}}(-\tilde{p}^{T}_{b,j}).

Missed positions are ordered by decreasing teacher mass and selected positions by increasing teacher mass. Rank-aligned pairs form the set 𝒱b\mathcal{V}_{b}; for i∈𝒱bi\in\mathcal{V}_{b}, the weights are

(6) ωb,i=sg⁡[max⁡(p~b,jb,i+T−p~b,jb,i−T,0)],i∈𝒱b.\omega_{b,i}=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\max\!\left(\tilde{p}^{T}_{b,j^{+}_{b,i}}-\tilde{p}^{T}_{b,j^{-}_{b,i}},0\right)\right],\quad i\in\mathcal{V}_{b}.

The batch-normalized loss is

(7) ℒaux=∑b∈ℬ∑i∈𝒱bωb,i​softplus⁡(sb,jb,i−S−sb,jb,i+S+δTrank)∑b∈ℬ∑i∈𝒱bωb,i+ϵ,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{b}}\omega_{b,i}\operatorname{softplus}\!\left(\frac{s^{S}_{b,j^{-}_{b,i}}-s^{S}_{b,j^{+}_{b,i}}+\delta}{T_{\mathrm{rank}}}\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{b}}\omega_{b,i}+\epsilon},

where the margin δ\delta encourages a missed positive’s student score to exceed its paired negative’s score by δ\delta, Trank>0T_{\mathrm{rank}}>0 controls the ranking scale, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 stabilizes the denominator. Invalid pairs are excluded through 𝒱b\mathcal{V}_{b}, and weights vanish whenever the teacher does not prefer the missed position. Mining and weights are detached, while gathered student logits remain differentiable. Thus each target contributes its own pairs without propagating gradients through discrete selection or into the teacher.

3.4. Target-Aware Retrieval and Aggregation

TWIN (Chang et al., 2023) uses consistent relevance-scoring parameters in its general and exact search units (GSU/ESU). We follow this strategy and extend parameter reuse to the full-history teacher: its learned query/key relevance parameters, denoted by Θrel\Theta_{\mathrm{rel}}, are exported to both TFR and the target-attention scorer.

Given ℋ~\widetilde{\mathcal{H}} and target vv, TFR selects MM records by their relevance scores using TWIN-style multi-head retrieval. Denote their positions by ℛvM\mathcal{R}^{M}_{v}. The retrieved records are then aggregated with TWIN-style target attention and fed into the final ranker.

3.5. Training Objectives

The selector graph trains the full-history teacher and DS with

(8) ℒsel=α​ℒpred+β​ℒKD+γ​ℒaux,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sel}}=\alpha\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}+\gamma\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}},

where ℒpred\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}} is the teacher’s multi-task prediction loss over behavior labels. The objective covers the whole selector graph: only ℒpred\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}} updates the teacher, while KD and auxiliary supervision train DS. Independent embeddings and detached teacher targets prevent student losses from updating the teacher. The teacher is therefore a live prediction branch rather than a separately pretrained, frozen model.

The ranking graph uses its own multi-task prediction objective ℒrank\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rank}}, with no additional distillation loss. Both graphs train on the same real-time dataset and share the intermediate store: the selector graph writes retained records and the ranking graph reads them. Algorithm 1 summarizes the two concurrent training processes.

3.6. Complexity Analysis

We separate training from online inference and count the main sequence-interaction operations, excluding feature projections, discrete selection/mining, store access, and the rest of the ranker. Let Hs,Ht,Hr,HaH_{s},H_{t},H_{r},H_{a} be the head counts of DS, teacher, retrieval, and aggregation. The corresponding widths ds,dt,dr,dad_{s},d_{t},d_{r},d_{a} reflect the operators actually executed; in particular, drd_{r} is the deployed per-head scoring width, and dad_{a} the per-head width used inside aggregation.

Training.

For a group of BB targets sharing one user’s length-LL history, DS scoring costs 𝒪⁡(L​Hs​ds)\mathcal{O}(LH_{s}d_{s}), while full-history teacher interactions cost 𝒪⁡(B​L​Ht​dt)\mathcal{O}(BLH_{t}d_{t}), with dtd_{t} covering teacher scoring and value aggregation. Distribution matching adds 𝒪⁡(B​L)\mathcal{O}(BL) and the loss over at most nn mined pairs adds 𝒪⁡(B​n)\mathcal{O}(Bn); these do not include pair mining itself. The ranking graph operates on the retained KK records. Thus training still includes length-dependent work, even though user-only computation is shared.

Online inference.

A request reads the stored KK records and evaluates CC targets. Its principal sequence-interaction cost is

(9) ΔECHO=𝒪⁡(C​Hr​K​dr)+𝒪⁡(C​Ha​M​da).\Delta_{\text{{ECHO}{}}}=\mathcal{O}(CH_{r}Kd_{r})+\mathcal{O}(CH_{a}Md_{a}).

The shared record read transfers 𝒪⁡(K)\mathcal{O}(K) data at fixed record width. Neither DS nor the full-history teacher executes online, so for fixed KK and MM the online branch is independent of the original history length LL. In contrast, applying direct target-aware retrieval, as in TWIN (Chang et al., 2023), to the full length-LL history incurs an interaction cost linear in both CC and LL.

3.7. Deployment Optimizations

Beyond the sequence budgets, deployment must control repeated feature processing, storage, and data movement. We use three complementary optimizations.

3.7.1. Common-feature sharing

We group multiple training samples from the same user within a batch and load their common user-side features, including the long behavior history, into GPU memory only once per user group. All samples in the group share this in-memory copy instead of materializing a separate copy for each user–target sample. This reduces the GPU memory occupied by duplicated common features, which is particularly costly for ultra-long histories. Target-specific features and computations remain sample-specific. This organization follows the user-level batching principle used by recent ultra-long-sequence systems (Guan et al., 2026b; Guan et al., 2026a).

3.7.2. Compact record encoding

The record schema depends on the application. In our production example, eight fields represented as int64 values require 8×8=648\times 8=64 bytes per event, or 640 KB at K=10,000K=10{,}000. Rather than reserving 64 bits for every field, we assign each field a fixed storage width sufficient for its value range and pack the fields consecutively into a record. The field widths are fixed by the application schema, not chosen separately for each event. In our deployed schema, the packed fields total 43 bytes per event, giving approximately 0.43 MB of record payload per user, about a third less than the int64 layout. The sequence is stored as one contiguous user-keyed value, enabling a single logical store operation. At a scale of one billion users, each with 10,00010{,}000 stored records, this encoding would reduce single-copy record payload from 640 TB to 430 TB, saving approximately 210 TB before replication and storage-system overhead.

3.7.3. Key-side projection absorption

Computing target–history relevance conventionally projects both query and history vectors. Since each history position requires a key projection, repeating this work for every request introduces sequence-length-dependent computation on the online path. Caching projected keys avoids repeated projection but requires a cache whose size also grows with the number of history positions. We instead transfer the key projection to the query side through the identity

(10) ⟨q​WQ,h​WK⟩=⟨(q​WQ)​WK⊤,h⟩.\langle qW_{Q},\;hW_{K}\rangle=\langle(qW_{Q})W_{K}^{\top},\;h\rangle.

This avoids explicitly projecting each retained history vector into a key and materializing the resulting per-position tensor, eliminating the need to maintain a projected-key cache.

4. Experiments

4.1. Experimental Settings

In this section, we evaluate the performance of ECHO using public and industrial datasets through a series of experiments, mainly to answer four research questions as follows:

  • •

    RQ1: How does ECHO perform compared to state-of-the-art methods on real-world datasets?

  • •

    RQ2: How effectively does ECHO select and preserve relevant behaviors from ultra-long user histories?

  • •

    RQ3: How efficiently does ECHO scale to longer user behavior sequences?

  • •

    RQ4: How do different components and hyperparameters affect ECHO’s performance?

Datasets and metrics.

We evaluate ECHO on the KuaiRand-1K benchmark (Gao et al., 2022) and Kuaishou’s industrial short-video recommendation platform, which is the largest recommendation scenario in Kuaishou and serves more than 400 million daily active users, generating over 50 billion interaction logs per day. For the KuaiRand-1K benchmark, we evaluate on four tasks: Click, Long-view, Like, and Comment. For the Kuaishou industrial dataset, we follow practical deployment requirements and focus on four key prediction tasks: Effective-view, Long-view, Like, and Comment. We adopt the GAUC (Zhou et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2026) to evaluate the performance of our model, which is the most critical offline metric in our short-video service. Notably, given the stability provided by the massive scale of training samples, a relative GAUC improvement of 0.05% is regarded as highly significant and can bring substantial business impact (Zhang et al., 2026).

Baselines.

We compare six representative sequence models: DIN (Zhou et al., 2018), SIM (Pi et al., 2020), TWIN (Chang et al., 2023), STCA (Guan et al., 2026b), TWIN V2 (Si et al., 2024), and SequenceO1 (Guan et al., 2026a). More details about baseline descriptions and implementation are provided in Appendix A.1 and Appendix A.2, respectively.

4.2. Overall Performance (RQ1)

Table 1 compares ECHO with six representative sequence modeling methods on KuaiRand-1K and the industrial dataset. ECHO consistently achieves the best GAUC across all eight prediction tasks, with relative improvements of 0.227%–1.520% on KuaiRand-1K and 0.113%–0.345% on the industrial dataset over the strongest baseline for each task. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of ECHO across different datasets and feedback objectives.

Among the baselines, search-based methods such as SIM and TWIN generally outperform DIN, which models only recent user behaviors, highlighting the importance of incorporating longer interaction histories for accurate user interest modeling. More advanced methods, including STCA, TWIN V2, and SequenceO1, achieve further improvements on several tasks through end-to-end long-sequence modeling or history compression. These results suggest that effectively exploiting historical information under constrained computational budgets is critical to improving recommendation performance as user behavior sequences grow longer.

ECHO further improves upon these methods across all tasks. In particular, on KuaiRand-1K, ECHO increases the Comment GAUC from 0.6252 to 0.6347, achieving a relative improvement of 1.520%. On the industrial dataset, the corresponding GAUC increases from 0.7824 to 0.7851, representing a 0.345% improvement. Unlike methods that truncate historical sequences or compress historical behaviors into aggregated representations, ECHO learns a user-level behavior selection strategy through target-aware distillation. This design reduces the online retrieval space while preserving original behavior records for fine-grained target matching. Furthermore, the shared relevance metric aligns the subsequent retrieval and interest aggregation stages, enabling ECHO to exploit prediction-relevant historical evidence within a bounded computational budget.

The improvements are also consistent across different feedback objectives. On KuaiRand-1K, ECHO achieves relative gains of 0.589% and 1.520% on Like and Comment, respectively. Similar improvements are observed on the industrial dataset, with gains of 0.297% and 0.345% on the corresponding tasks. ECHO also improves viewing-related predictions, achieving relative gains of 0.113% on Effective-view and 0.119% on Long-view in the industrial dataset. These results demonstrate that the benefits of ECHO extend beyond specific interaction signals, supporting its effectiveness across diverse recommendation objectives.

4.3. Selected History Analysis (RQ2)

To understand how ECHO benefits from ultra-long user histories, we investigate the effectiveness of the Distilled Selector (DS) from three perspectives: downstream prediction performance, preservation of relevant historical behaviors, and sensitivity to the selection budget. We compare DS with recency-based truncation and uniform random selection, using the target-aware teacher as a reference for evaluating the quality of retained historical evidence.

We first examine how the benefit of learned selection varies with history length. As shown in Figure 2, ECHO consistently outperforms TWIN with a recent 10K history, and the improvement becomes more pronounced as the available history grows. Specifically, the relative GAUC gain increases from 0.045% for histories shorter than 10K to 1.279% for histories exceeding 50K. This trend suggests that a fixed recent-history window increasingly overlooks useful historical evidence as user behaviors accumulate, whereas ECHO can identify relevant interactions from a broader history. The advantage persists under smaller sequence budgets. With retention and retrieval budgets of 5K and 50, respectively, ECHO achieves a GAUC of 0.6618, compared with 0.6603 for recent-5K TWIN. Even when the budgets are reduced to 2K and 20, ECHO maintains an improvement from 0.6585 to 0.6599. These results indicate that the effectiveness of ECHO stems not only from accessing longer histories, but also from allocating the limited sequence budget to more informative behaviors.

We next investigate whether DS successfully preserves the historical behaviors favored by the target-aware teacher. Figure 3(a) reports the recall of the teacher’s Top-100 relevant behaviors within the 10K retained events. DS achieves an average recall of 99.976%, substantially outperforming recency-based and random selection, which achieve 57.905% and 49.443%, respectively. Notably, its recall remains above 99.9% across all history-length groups, while recency-based selection deteriorates considerably as history length increases. Figure 3(b) further evaluates the proportion of the teacher’s relevance distribution preserved by the selected events. DS retains 98.509% of the total relevance mass on average, compared with only 55.913% for recency-based selection, and maintains 95.74% even for the longest histories. These results demonstrate that target-aware distillation enables the candidate-agnostic selector to preserve most of the historical evidence emphasized by the teacher, despite substantially reducing the searchable history.

We further analyze the temporal distribution of selected behaviors and their agreement with the teacher. As illustrated in Figure 4, 46.08% of the behaviors retained by DS fall outside the most recent 10K interactions, with this proportion increasing to 75.09% for the longest-history group. This confirms that DS does not simply approximate recency-based truncation, but actively selects informative interactions from older portions of the history. Meanwhile, Figure 5(a) compares DS and the teacher under identical Top-kk selection budgets. Their overlap reaches 67.58% at k=100k=100 and 82.45% at k=10​Kk=10K. Together with the near-perfect recall of the teacher’s Top-100 behaviors within the retained 10K events, these findings suggest that DS need not reproduce the teacher’s exact fine-grained ranking. Instead, it can preserve a sufficiently broad set of relevant original behaviors, allowing the subsequent target-aware retriever to perform more precise matching for each candidate.

Finally, we investigate how effectively DS preserves attention mass under different retention budgets. As shown in Figure 5(b), using the teacher’s Top-10K behaviors as the reference, DS captures 70.84%, 91.65%, and 99.38% of the reference attention mass with retention budgets of 100, 1K, and 10K, respectively. In contrast, recency-based selection retains only 0.43%, 5.14%, and 55.93% under the same budgets. The substantial gap indicates that learned selection can concentrate teacher-attended historical evidence into a much smaller subset of original behavior records. This property is particularly important for ECHO’s cascaded design: the user-level selector reduces the searchable history while preserving high-relevance events, and the subsequent target-aware retriever performs fine-grained matching within the retained set. Overall, these results validate the effectiveness of distillation-guided selection in balancing historical evidence preservation and bounded online retrieval costs.

4.4. Efficiency and Length Scaling (RQ3)

To evaluate the computational efficiency and scalability of ECHO for ultra-long user behavior modeling, we compare it with STCA, an end-to-end long-sequence modeling method, in terms of computational cost and predictive performance. STCA directly models historical behaviors through stacked target-aware attention layers, whereas ECHO adopts a cascaded architecture that combines user-level behavior selection with target-aware retrieval, restricting downstream computation to a bounded set of historical events. We estimate the training and inference FLOPs based on the sequence modeling architectures of both methods, with detailed calculations and configuration assumptions provided in Appendix A.3.

Figures 6(a) and (b) illustrate the computational costs of both methods as the history length increases. While the training and inference costs of STCA grow substantially with sequence length, ECHO exhibits much slower growth. This advantage stems from decoupling user-level behavior selection from candidate-dependent interest modeling, allowing subsequent retrieval and attention operations to process only a bounded number of historical events. At a history length of 100K, ECHO reduces the estimated sequence-branch FLOPs by approximately 160.3× and 159.2× during training and inference, respectively, compared with STCA. These results demonstrate the computational efficiency of the cascaded architecture when scaling to ultra-long behavior sequences.

We further investigate how predictive performance scales with history length. As shown in Figure 6(c), both ECHO and STCA achieve consistent GAUC improvements as the available history length increases, indicating that longer histories provide additional information for user interest modeling. Specifically, the GAUC of ECHO increases from 0.6614 at 10K to 0.6630 at 50K, while STCA improves from 0.6598 at 5K to 0.6645 at 50K. Although STCA has a slight advantage at longer histories by directly modeling the full history, ECHO continues to benefit from longer sequences by preserving informative historical behaviors through its distilled selector and performing target-aware retrieval within a bounded sequence budget.

Overall, ECHO effectively reduces candidate-dependent sequence computation while retaining the predictive benefits of long-history modeling. By shifting history selection to a reusable user-level stage, ECHO enables efficient access to increasingly long behavior histories without requiring full-history target-aware interactions for every candidate. These results highlight its potential for scalable ultra-long sequence modeling under the computational constraints of industrial recommendation systems.

4.5. Ablation Study (RQ4)

We evaluate ECHO by ablating its training objectives, distillation temperature, and downstream ranking architectures.

To examine the contribution of distillation supervision, we remove both the knowledge distillation loss ℒK​D\mathcal{L}_{KD} and the boundary-targeted auxiliary loss ℒa​u​x\mathcal{L}_{aux}, equip the student with an independent prediction head, and train it using prediction loss alone. As shown in Table 2, the full ECHO model consistently outperforms the prediction-only variant across all four tasks on KuaiRand-1K, achieving relative GAUC improvements of 0.272%, 0.925%, 2.371%, and 0.317% on Click, Like, Comment, and Long-view, respectively. The largest improvement is observed on Comment, where GAUC increases from 0.6200 to 0.6347. These results demonstrate the importance of distillation-based supervision for effective history selection. By transferring target-aware relevance knowledge from the teacher to the user-level selector, the distillation objective guides the preservation of informative historical behaviors, while the boundary-targeted auxiliary objective further encourages teacher-preferred events to be included in the retained set. Together, these objectives improve history selection and downstream predictions.

Furthermore, we investigate the sensitivity of ECHO to the distillation temperature and evaluate its applicability across different downstream architectures. Due to space limitations, detailed experimental results are provided in Appendix A.4.

4.6. Online A/B Testing

To assess the practical effectiveness of ECHO, we conduct a seven-day online A/B test in the Kuaishou short-video recommendation scenario described above, with 5% of production traffic assigned to the treatment bucket.

Notably, the existing production system already incorporates advanced long-sequence modeling techniques, including TWIN-based behavior retrieval and sequence compression mechanisms similar to C-Former and SequenceO1. Rather than replacing a simple short-history baseline, ECHO is integrated into this established recommendation system to further enhance the utilization of ultra-long user histories. During online inference, the ranking system reads the retained historical records and performs target-aware retrieval and interest aggregation, while the user-level selector is maintained by the real-time training pipeline. The deployment is further supported by shared user inputs, compact record encoding, and key-side projection absorption, as detailed in Section 3.7. Compared with the existing production systems, ECHO achieved +0.240% and +0.373% increases in Total App Usage Time on Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite, respectively, demonstrating its benefit to user engagement in production environments.

5. Conclusion

In this paper, we propose ECHO, a distillation-guided framework for ultra-long user behavior sequence modeling in industrial recommendation systems. ECHO employs a user-level Distilled Selector to identify and retain informative original behavior records from user histories of up to 100K events, followed by a Target-aware Fine-grained Retriever for downstream interest modeling. Through target-aware distillation and relevance parameter sharing, ECHO reduces candidate-dependent computation while preserving fine-grained matching capabilities over historical behaviors. We conducted extensive experiments on KuaiRand-1K and an industrial dataset. ECHO achieves the best GAUC across all eight prediction tasks. Further analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of the distilled selector in preserving highly relevant historical behaviors, as well as the computational efficiency and scalability of ECHO for ultra-long sequence modeling. Moreover, we conducted seven-day online A/B tests in two production scenarios, Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite. Compared with the existing production systems, ECHO achieved +0.240% and +0.373% increases in Total App Usage Time, respectively, demonstrating the practical effectiveness of ECHO in large-scale recommendation systems.

Appendix A Additional Experimental Details

A.1. Baselines

To comprehensively evaluate ECHO, we compare it with six representative user behavior sequence modeling methods, categorized according to how they process historical interactions.

(1) Short-history modeling. DIN (Zhou et al., 2018) employs target-aware attention to capture user interests from recent interactions. Due to the computational cost of attention over long sequences, it typically models a limited window of recent behaviors.

(2) Retrieval-based long-sequence modeling. SIM (Pi et al., 2020) introduces a two-stage framework consisting of a General Search Unit (GSU) and an Exact Search Unit (ESU), which first retrieves target-relevant behaviors from long-term histories and then performs fine-grained interest modeling. TWIN (Chang et al., 2023) further aligns the relevance metrics between the GSU and ESU, addressing the inconsistency between retrieval and downstream interest modeling.

(3) End-to-end long-sequence modeling. STCA (Guan et al., 2026b) employs stacked target-aware cross-attention layers, together with batching optimizations and sequence-length extrapolation, to efficiently model user behavior histories at the 10K scale.

(4) Compression-based ultra-long sequence modeling. TWIN V2 (Si et al., 2024) compresses lifelong user behaviors into cluster-structured representations and performs cluster-aware target attention to extend the range of historical interactions available for modeling. SequenceO1 (Guan et al., 2026a) constructs a fixed-size user history sketch and combines low-rank caching with recent-history modeling, enabling efficient modeling of user behavior sequences at the 100K scale while bounding candidate-dependent computation.

A.2. Implementation Details

In offline experiments, we configure the history length of each method according to its modeling characteristics. For DIN, the maximum history length is set to 100. For SIM and TWIN, the input history length of the General Search Unit (GSU) is limited to 10K behaviors. STCA is trained with an average sequence length of 2K and extrapolates to 10K during inference. TWIN V2 clusters the most recent 50K behaviors into approximately 10K representative units. SequenceO1 compresses the same behaviors into a fixed-size sketch of 100 tokens and uses cache reuse to support ultra-long sequence modeling. For ECHO, the maximum raw history length is set to 50K, from which the Distilled Selector (DS) retains 10K original behavior records for downstream target-aware retrieval. For all two-stage retrieval methods, the final retrieval budget is set to 100 behaviors for subsequent interest modeling.

In industrial online deployment, we further extend the maximum raw history length of ECHO to 100K behaviors to accommodate ultra-long user histories in real-world recommendation scenarios. The DS retains 10K original behavior records, while the Target-aware Fine-grained Retriever (TFR) retrieves 100 relevant behaviors for each candidate item. This configuration expands the accessible history range while keeping the downstream retrieval and interest modeling budgets fixed.

All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A800 GPUs using a hybrid distributed training framework. For KuaiRand-1K, we adopt the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3} and a batch size of 256. For the industrial dataset, both sparse embedding parameters and dense network parameters are optimized using Adam, with learning rates of 0.0010.001 and 0.00050.0005, respectively, and a batch size of 3,000.

A.3. Computational Cost Analysis

We provide the analytical FLOPs estimates used in Fig. 6(a) and (b). We count dense matrix operations, with one multiply–accumulate equal to two FLOPs. Let LL denote the history length, K=min⁡(L,10,000)K=\min(L,10{,}000) the retention budget, and RR the number of candidates sharing the same user history. Candidate-independent computations are amortized over RR, while target-dependent operations are counted per candidate. We set Rtr=40R_{\mathrm{tr}}=40 and Rinf=300R_{\mathrm{inf}}=300, with assumed selection-cache hit rates htr=0.5h_{\mathrm{tr}}=0.5 and hinf=0.6h_{\mathrm{inf}}=0.6. Cached selections are reused only for unchanged selector versions and history snapshots, while trainable attention activations are recomputed at each training step.

STCA

We reconstruct the single-query attention reordering and fusion architecture of STCA (Guan et al., 2026b) with m=4m=4 layers, hidden width d=128d=128, H=4H=4 heads, and SwiGLU expansion ratio r=4r=4. Under reordered attention, each head performs scoring and weighted reduction over the original dd-dimensional history, contributing 4​m​H​L​d4mHLd FLOPs. The remaining query-side projections and fusion operations contribute

+2​(m+1)​d2+F\displaystyle+2(m+1)d^{2}+F

=1,572,864​LR+8,192​L+2,949,120.\displaystyle=\frac{1{,}572{,}864L}{R}+8{,}192L+2{,}949{,}120.

ECHO

The counted ECHO computation consists of amortized selector refresh and retained-history attention. The frozen selector uses a 624→128624\rightarrow 128 input projection and grouped query-side transformations of 128→256→185128\rightarrow 256\rightarrow 185, where the final dimension includes a bias coordinate. The input projection precedes user grouping, while the subsequent transformations and history scan are shared. With linear history-side projections absorbed into the query side, the expected refresh cost is

(13) S⁡(L,R,h)=(1−h)​[159,744+160,256+370​LR],S(L,R,h)=(1-h)\left[159{,}744+\frac{160{,}256+370L}{R}\right],

where the three terms correspond to the input projection, grouped query-side transformations, and history scan. The frozen selector incurs only forward computation when a refresh is required. This represents amortized user-state maintenance rather than per-candidate selector execution during online ranking.

The retained-history attention layer uses four heads with total width 128 and a 256-dimensional target query. Including query projection, shared key/value projections, and target-aware scoring and aggregation over KK events, its forward cost is

(14) A⁡(K,R)\displaystyle A(K,R) =2⋅256⋅128+4⋅185⋅128​KR+4⋅128​K\displaystyle=2\cdot 256\cdot 128+\frac{4\cdot 185\cdot 128K}{R}+4\cdot 128K
=65,536+94,720​KR+512​K.\displaystyle=65{,}536+\frac{94{,}720K}{R}+512K.

Absorbing the input transformation into the key/value projections requires a parameter composition cost of P=4⋅185⋅256⋅128=24,248,320P=4\cdot 185\cdot 256\cdot 128=24{,}248{,}320 FLOPs. These parameters are precomputed for inference but recomposed during training. With UU user groups per microbatch, the amortized cost is P/(U​R)P/(UR) per target, we set U=1U=1.

Training and inference costs.

We approximate forward and backward computation for trainable matrix operations as three times the forward FLOPs, while frozen selector refresh remains forward-only. The total estimated costs are

A.4. Additional Experimental Results

We investigate the sensitivity of ECHO to the distillation temperature TT, which controls the smoothness of the teacher’s relevance distribution and consequently affects the supervision provided to the selector. We vary TT over {1,2,4,6,8}\{1,2,4,6,8\} and evaluate Click GAUC on KuaiRand-1K. As illustrated in Figure 7, GAUC increases from 0.6617 at T=1T=1 to 0.6630 at T=4T=4, before decreasing to 0.6613 at T=8T=8. This indicates that the sharpness of the distillation distribution plays an important role in learning effective behavior selection. A lower temperature concentrates supervision on a small number of highly relevant behaviors, potentially overlooking useful relevance information from other interactions. Conversely, an excessively high temperature produces a smoother distribution that may weaken the distinction between behaviors of different relevance levels. An intermediate temperature provides a better balance between emphasizing highly relevant behaviors and preserving richer relevance information, leading to improved prediction performance.

Finally, we evaluate the applicability of ECHO across different downstream ranking architectures. Since ECHO performs user-level history selection while preserving original behavior records, its selection mechanism can be integrated with different feature interaction networks. We compare ECHO with TWIN using three downstream backbones: MLP, RankMixer, and MixFormer. As shown in Figure 8, ECHO consistently outperforms TWIN across all three architectures, achieving relative GAUC improvements of 0.15%–0.35% on Click and 0.09%–0.35% on Long-view. In particular, ECHO improves Click GAUC from 0.6607 to 0.6630 with MLP and from 0.6629 to 0.6640 with MixFormer. Despite variations in improvement across backbones, the consistent gains across all six comparisons indicate that ECHO can provide informative historical evidence for different downstream models, demonstrating its flexibility and model-agnostic applicability.

Overall, these experiments validate the effectiveness of distillation-based supervision, highlight the importance of an appropriate distillation temperature, and demonstrate that ECHO can effectively complement diverse downstream ranking architectures.

Appendix B Limitations

Long-tail limitations.

Compressing 100K events to 10K may discard history relevant to extremely long-tail targets, making it unavailable to downstream retrieval. Unlike SequenceO1 (Guan et al., 2026a), which compresses sequences into tokens, ECHO retains original records, allowing direct access to item identities, timestamps, and side features when relevant events survive selection and are retrieved. However, long-tail items can still be discarded during compression.

Adaptation latency.

The selector adapts through training, not to individual online targets. Recovering excluded events for long-tail targets requires relevant training signals, model updates, and selection refreshes.
